title: Hand planing
subtitle: How to set up and use a bench plane for flat and smooth surfaces on seasoned timber
excerpt: Hand planing produces a smoother surface than sandpaper and removes material faster than any other hand tool. Done correctly, the plane cuts with the grain and produces a surface that is flat, smooth, and ready for finishing. Done wrong, the blade chatters, the surface tears, or the plane digs in and leaves hollows. This guide covers setting up the plane, reading grain direction, and controlling the cut.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the bench plane setting and use; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the grain-reading and blade-adjustment method.

glossaryTerms.definition: Planing in the direction the wood fibres run from the wood surface downward. Cuts with the grain are smooth; cuts against the grain lift and tear fibres.
The upper blade in a bench plane, also called the cap iron. Its job is to curl and break the shaving before it can tear a large chip ahead of the blade.
The gap between the blade edge and the front of the plane sole opening. A narrow throat limits how much shaving the plane takes and reduces tear-out.

content.text: A well-tuned bench plane is one of the most productive tools in the workshop. A No. 5 jack plane is the right first plane for the projects in this sub-category: it is long enough to bridge minor hollows and remove them, and short enough to be controlled on small boards. Setting the plane correctly takes five minutes; the technique takes an afternoon to feel natural.
When to use this technique

Whenever a seasoned timber board needs a flat, smooth face for a board, shelf, panel, or rack back. For boards larger than 20 cm by 5 cm, a plane is faster and produces a better result than sandpaper alone.
Setting the blade depth

Hold the plane upside down and sight along the sole toward a light source. The blade edge should project slightly, about the thickness of a sheet of paper, beyond the sole. Adjust the depth with the depth adjuster wheel: clockwise to extend the blade, anti-clockwise to retract. For a light smoothing cut, less projection; for a heavier roughing cut, more projection. Start with the blade barely visible and increase depth until the plane takes a clean, thin shaving.
Checking the blade lateral alignment

The blade must be perpendicular to the sole, if it is skewed, the plane cuts a deeper shaving on one side and skips on the other. Check by sighting the blade from the front of the plane: the edge should be parallel to the sole line. Adjust with the lateral adjustment lever.
The
chip-breaker
should sit within 0.5 mm of the blade edge. Set it further back and the unsupported blade flexes on the cut, causing chatter. The
throat
is the gap between the blade and the front of the sole opening. On a No. 5 the factory setting suits most work.
Reading grain direction
On most boards the grain runs in one direction along the face. Look at the edge of the board: the grain lines slope either left or right from the face. Plane
with the grain

, in the direction the lines slope downward into the board face. If you plane the wrong way, the shavings come off in broken pieces and the surface has a rough, lifted texture. Reverse direction and the surface becomes glassy.
Planing technique

Start the stroke with pressure on the front of the plane (the toe). As the plane traverses the board, shift pressure to the heel. Lift the plane on the return stroke rather than dragging it, dragging dulls the blade on the return. Use the full length of the plane in each stroke: this bridges any hollow in the board and removes the high spots first, automatically flattening the surface.
Checking flatness

Place a straightedge diagonally across the surface in both diagonal directions. Light showing under the straightedge indicates a hollow; darkness all the way across indicates a flat section. Repeat the check at several positions. Mark high spots with pencil crosses and work on these with the next planing pass.

attrs.symptom: The plane chatters, a rapid vibration that leaves a rippled surface
attrs.cause: The blade is projecting too much, or the chip breaker is set too far back from the cutting edge, leaving too much unsupported blade
attrs.fix: Retract the blade depth. Set the chip breaker within 0.5 mm of the blade edge, a chip breaker set more than 1 mm back allows the shaving to lever the blade tip, causing chatter. Tighten the plane cap screw firmly.

attrs.symptom: The surface tears no matter which direction the plane is used
attrs.cause: Interlocked grain, the grain direction reverses across the face of the board
attrs.fix: Plane diagonally across the board at 45 degrees to the grain direction. A diagonal pass always goes at least partly with the grain, regardless of which way the grain twists. Follow with a light finishing pass at the grain angle identified in the least-torn section.
